sources_considered.why: Fixed pre-publication benchmark version documents recurring errors and important task-dependent limitations.

evidence_items.explanation: The February benchmark release reports substantial errors across proprietary and open-weight model families on difficult multi-turn legal, research, medical, and coding tasks. It supports recurring fabrication in those settings, but does not estimate ordinary-use frequency or establish every listed harm.

evidence_items.publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence_items.explanation: The March publication reports clinically relevant errors across evaluated models, including a 29.1% rate for its best performer. Its tests deliberately inject hallucination traps, and the accessible abstract does not date the underlying experiments; it is therefore supporting context rather than decisive evidence of current ordinary-use frequency.

evidence_items.locator: Section I, Pure Fabrication; discussion of Walters v. OpenAI
evidence_items.explanation: The summary describes ChatGPT inventing an embezzlement accusation against Mark Walters, but the incident predates the target period. It also explains that OpenAI won summary judgment, so fabricated reputational content must not be equated with established legal liability.

The paper finds meaningful variation across models and tasks and discusses much lower rates on easier evaluations. This limits extrapolation from its difficult benchmark to a general claim about frequency.

unresolved_gaps: The inspected evidence does not establish representative ordinary-use frequency across essentially all major providers.
No authenticated set of reputational falsehoods from the target period establishes the claim’s full contemporary scope.
The medical abstract does not identify when its underlying experiments occurred.
The benchmark evidence does not supply a complete census of the providers and systems implicated by the wording.
